newsitem.title: UK: Bank gold sales-less bearish when they've happened.
newsitem.headline: Bank gold sales-less bearish when they've happened.

text.p: The bullion market has seen seven big central bank gold sales since 1989, but official word of these, when finally announced, has tended not to provoke steep new price falls.
It has been the anticipation of such sales that has seemed to depress sentiment and has hurt prices ahead of actual confirmation, dealers said.
"There are usually leaks and lots of speculation. Concrete signs like borrowing rates rising put dealers on their guard," one analyst said.
The announcement of the sale invariably follows the actual disposal so that the bullion price may already have been influenced by fresh metal coming into the market, another analyst suggested.
The major gold disposals since 1989, until news on Thursday of an Australian sale, have involved either the Belgian or Dutch central banks.
The Dutch most recently announced the sale of 300 tonnes of gold in January this year. Their previous sale was in 1992-1993 when they and the Belgian National Bank together sold 602 tonnes.
Belgium subsequently sold 175 tonnes in 1995 and 203 tonnes during the first quarter of 1996. It made its first major gold sale in 1989 when it disposed of 127 tonnes.
The first Belgian sale was announced on March 22 1989 when the PM London gold fix was $393.35 per ounce. On March 29, the fix was $382.95.
The Belgian announcement of a 202-tonne sale on June 27, 1992 had less impact. The fix went from $342.00 on June 17 to $342.30 seven days later.
The Dutch announcement of a 400-tonne sale on January 12, 1993 moved the gold fix from $329.20 to $329.00 on January 19.
Belgium's announcement of a 175-tonne sale on April 24, 1995 came when the fix was $390.65. On May 1 gold fixed at $387.20.
Belgium's last sale of 203 tonnes was announced on March 27, 1996 when the fix was $400.35 and it had slipped to $394.65 on April 3.
The Belgian Central Bank has sold 707 tonnes of gold since its disposal programme began in 1989.
Canada's central bank through a programme of small monthly disposals has sold 592 tonnes since 1979.
Last year research organisation Gold Fields Mineral Services (GFMS) calculated there was a net sale of 239 tonnes of bullion from reserves by official sector holders.
The net figure comprised 588 tonnes of gross disposals and 349 tonnes of gross purchases.
The average for the past 10 years is a net disposal of 213 tonnes, according to GFMS.
In 1996 16 countries were net sellers of gold but only five sold more than 10 tonnes.
Central banks bought gold for their reserves in 1996 with Russia and China the most prominent buyers, GMFS said.
